name: Hana Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for agreeing to talk. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not connected to any company, union, party or government. Everything here is confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a tablet press at a medicine factory that makes generic painkillers and allergy pills. Powder goes in the top, the press squeezes it into tablets, thousands a minute, and I check weight, hardness and thickness every half hour and write it into the batch record. Everything is gowned up and super clean. I've been there eight months, and I'm still slower than the others at a changeover because the cleaning checks are so strict.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it matters, people actually swallow what we make. I use an AI chatbot every day, mostly to study the regulations, because I want to move into quality checking. What wears me out is the paperwork, honestly, and twelve-hour shifts in a gown.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, the tools are useful and nobody lost their head. I'd keep telling people at work how I use the chatbot to study. I'd post a little about it, but nothing preachy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means my plan works as it is. I want to move from the press to quality checking in a couple of years. I've got my own flat with a small mortgage, help from my father on the deposit, and about eight months saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep running the press and keep studying for the quality technician certificate in the evenings. Keep helping my mum's spice business at weekends, I do her online listings. Put a bit more into savings each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pleased, actually, because steady suits a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about your mum's spice business.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum blends spices at home, and I use AI to write the product descriptions for her online shop. She sells at the Saturday market too. It's not big money, but it's family, and it's growing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that bothers you about work in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The generic medicine business is tight on prices. If a big buyer goes to a cheaper factory abroad, we could lose a shift. That's an old worry, not a new one.

say: I'd say the tools are **useful** and nobody lost their head.
I'd keep telling colleagues how I use a **chatbot** to study.
think: My plan to move from the press to **quality checking** still works.
My **own flat**, small mortgage and eight months saved keep me secure.
do: Study for the **quality technician** certificate in the evenings.
Keep doing **online listings** for her mother's spice business at weekends.
feel: She feels **calm** and **pleased**, because steady suits a plan.
S0.quote: My mum blends spices at home, and I use AI to write the product descriptions for her online shop.
fieldNote: She has a clear **career plan** towards quality checking.
Family matters: she runs her mother's **spice shop** online.
Her real worry is **price pressure** on generic medicines, not AI.

steps.text: Study evenings for the quality technician certificate
Run her mother's online spice shop listings at weekends
Add a bit more to savings each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a great time to be someone who learns fast. At work I'd offer to show people how to use the tools. Online I'd say families and firms should train people, not wait for the government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be careful. Quality checking is a lot of reading batch records and spotting errors, which is exactly the checking work the card mentions. So the job I'm aiming for might shrink. But medicine factories change slowly because every new machine has to be approved, which buys time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still go for the quality technician certificate, but aim for the part that's on the floor, like sampling and checking equipment. Learn the AI tools the quality team uses, so I'm the one who runs them. Grow the spice shop a little.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A little alert, like when the press makes a new noise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at the factory?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The ladies in documentation who type up batch records. That's going to be software within a few years. I'd want the firm to train them, because they know the rules better than anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You lean towards firms and families helping, not government. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because my dad came here with nothing and family and work got him through. I'm not against all help, but I'd rather a firm trains you than a cheque sits you at home.

I'd say **families and firms** should train people, not wait for the government.
think: Quality checking is mostly **reading records**, so my target job might shrink.
Medicine factories change **slowly** because every new machine needs approval.
do: Aim for the **floor-based** side of quality: sampling and equipment checks.
Learn the **AI tools** the quality team uses so she runs them.
S1.quote: Medicine factories change slowly because every new machine has to be approved, which buys time.
fieldNote: She spots that her **target role** is thinking work and adjusts towards the floor.

Her outlook rests on her father's **migrant work ethic**.

steps.text: Aim the quality certificate at sampling and equipment checks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is huge, and people should start preparing tonight, not wait for anyone. I'd say families need to pull together. I'd share practical advice online about what skills still matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, by 2028 the AI can do the quality paperwork better than any person, so my plan dies. Then in 2031 a robot could run the tablet press, though medicine rules might slow it a year or two. So I've got maybe three to five years on the press, and nowhere obvious to climb.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd switch from studying quality to studying maintenance, because someone has to fix and clean those robots under strict rules. I'd grow the spice business seriously, with my mum, because family food is something people will still buy from people. I'd keep the flat and pay the mortgage down fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'm not panicking, I've got a plan, but my nice neat plan would be gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said medicine rules might slow the robots. Are you counting on that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little, yes, but I wouldn't bet my flat on it. Rules can change fast if the government wants cheaper medicine. I'd use the extra time if it comes, but plan as if it doesn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my parents the spice shop might end up being the real family job. My dad would laugh, but he'd also start building shelves.

say: I'd say people should start **preparing tonight**, not wait for anyone.
I'd say **families** need to pull together, and share practical skills advice online.
think: By **2028** AI does quality paperwork better than people, so my plan dies.
Robots could run the press by **2031**, maybe later due to medicine rules.
do: Switch from quality study to **maintenance** training for clean-room robots.
Grow the **spice business** seriously with her mother.
feel: She feels **anxious** but not panicking, because her **neat plan** is gone.
S2.quote: I'd tell my parents the spice shop might end up being the real family job.
fieldNote: She separates **2028** (her target role goes) from **2031** (her current role goes).
She **refuses to bet** on regulation slowing robots, though she hopes it will.
Family business becomes a real **fallback**, not a hobby.

steps.text: Switch her evening study to clean-room equipment maintenance
Grow her mum's spice business into a real income
Make extra payments on the flat's mortgage
Work with her parents to build the spice shop together

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if you start now. I'd tell my cousins to pick skills that need hands and judgement together. I'd help anyone at work who wanted to learn the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is workable. I could get the quality certificate, use it for a few years, and then switch to maintenance around 2030. The robots come in 2034, maybe later in medicine, and by then I'd have two skills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Finish the quality certificate next year, then start maintenance training around 2029. Grow the spice shop steadily, maybe rent a small kitchen unit with my mum. Keep using AI for studying and for the shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I can see how it works, but it's a lot of moving parts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave the medicine factory?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if I had something solid. The pay is good and it's a respectable job, my parents are proud of it. I'd rather change roles inside the factory than walk out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What worries you most in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Doing everything at once and burning out. Studying, a shop and twelve-hour shifts is a lot, and my mum would tell me to slow down. She'd be right.

say: I'd say **five years** is enough if you start now.
I'd tell cousins to pick skills needing **hands and judgement** together.
think: Five years is **workable**: quality first, then maintenance around 2030.
By **2034** I'd have two skills, and medicine may be slower still.
do: Finish the **quality certificate** next year, then start maintenance training around 2029.
Rent a small **kitchen unit** with her mother for the spice shop.
feel: She feels **uneasy** about the many **moving parts**.
S3.quote: Studying, a shop and twelve-hour shifts is a lot, and my mum would tell me to slow down.
fieldNote: With five years she can **stack** quality and maintenance skills.

steps.text: Finish the quality technician certificate next year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, so use it. I'd say firms should train their own people and families should back each other. I'd keep sharing how I learn with AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, this is the good one for me. I'd have ten years to build a career and the spice business both. By 2039 I'd be 40, with a maintenance ticket, a paid-off chunk of the flat and a family business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get the quality certificate, then maintenance, and maybe a supervisor role in the mid-2030s. Grow the spice shop into a proper brand with my mum and my brother. Maybe get married, if the right person comes along, my parents keep asking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Hopeful, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you change course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the medicine rules changed and robots came early. I'd keep an eye on what the bigger factories are doing. I'd move earlier if I saw it coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for the next generation in your family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want my nieces to learn a skill they can do with their hands and their heads, and to stay close to family. Those two things don't go out of date.

say: I'd say **ten years** is a gift, so use it.
I'd say firms should **train their own** people and families should back each other.
think: This is the **good one** for me, with time for a career and the business.
By **2039** I'd have a maintenance ticket and a family business.
do: Get the quality certificate, then **maintenance**, then maybe a supervisor role.
Grow the spice shop into a **proper brand** with her mother and brother.
S4.quote: I'd want my nieces to learn a skill they can do with their hands and their heads, and to stay close to family.
fieldNote: With a decade, she's **calm**: careers and family business both have time.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. My plan to move into quality would die before I finished studying for it. What would help is firms paying for maintenance and robot training for their own staff, before they bring the robots in.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about family businesses. People will still want to buy food from a real family, even when robots make the pills.

headlineQuote: People will still want to buy food from a real family, even when robots make the pills.
portrait: Hana is a **27-year-old** tablet press operator at a generic medicine factory, eight months in.
She owns a flat with a small mortgage and has **eight months** saved.
She uses **AI daily** to study and runs her mother's online spice shop.
AGI by 2028 kills her **quality plan**, so she turns to maintenance and the family business.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because her **quality plan** would die before she finished studying.
whatWouldHelp: Firms paying for **maintenance and robot** training for their own staff before robots arrive.
